proposed_edges.relationship: Israel argues that Pocock's ‘family of enlightenments’ in Barbarism and Religion underestimates what the national strands shared and how far they fall into radical and moderate currents, and that Pocock's ecclesiastical emphasis undermines his own case for pluralism (Journal of the History of Ideas, 2016)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read 2026-10-31: author abstract (Crossref-deposited, as printed) of Israel, ‘J. G. A. Pocock and the “Language of Enlightenment” in His Barbarism and Religion’, JHI 77:1 (2016): 107–127. Pocock ‘argues for a “family of enlightenments,” disputing accounts, particularly Venturi’s and Gay’s, of it as a unified phenomenon’; Israel ‘asserts, however, that Pocock’s reconfiguration of different national contexts … underestimates their commonality and the degree to which they fall into the recognizable currents of radical and moderate’; ‘Pocock’s attention to the ecclesiastical and theological dimensions of the Enlightenment undermines rather than supports his argument for its pluralism.’ Context, read: Wolin's symposium introduction abstract (JHI 77:1, 99–106) places the essay in a symposium that ends with ‘a concluding response by Pocock’, arising from a CUNY conference in 2010; John Robertson's review of Barbarism and Religion I–II (Cromohs 6, 2001) had already written that ‘Pocock's Enlightenment is directly opposed to that with which Jonathan Israel has just presented us’. Article body and Pocock's response unread (Project MUSE challenge page). The edge is Israel's critique; Pocock's reply is not represented.

review.reason: Crossref-deposited author abstract re-read verbatim: Pocock argues for 'a “family of enlightenments,” disputing accounts, particularly Venturi’s and Gay’s'; Pocock's reconfiguration 'underestimates their commonality and the degree to which they fall into the recognizable currents of radical and moderate'; ecclesiastical attention 'undermines rather than supports his argument for its pluralism'. Wolin abstract confirms the symposium and Pocock's concluding response; Cromohs (open journal) contains 'Pocock’s Enlightenment is directly opposed to that with which Jonathan Israel has just presented us'. Abstract-only reading is declared in the evidence note and the relationship does not go beyond the abstract. Accept.

proposed_edges.relationship: Israel charges that Darnton, with other social and cultural historians of the Enlightenment, ‘hardly engage[s] with ideas at all’, citing Darnton's neglect of d'Holbach's place at the top of his own lists of clandestine best-sellers (H-France Forum response, 2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words, read 2026-10-31: Israel, response essay, H-France Forum 9:1 (Winter 2014), no. 5, on Democratic Enlightenment (2011). P. 85: ‘Darnton, Chartier, Jacob, Goodman, Roche, Lilti, and others err in my estimation not in claiming ideas are refracted, modified, used selectively, ignored, and twisted—that is all too true, but because they hardly engage with ideas at all’; ‘A striking instance … is Darnton’s treatment of d’Holbach whose books regularly topped his lists of the most widely selling clandestine texts, an astounding fact which, however, he completely ignores’ (n. 25 cites Darnton, The Corpus of Clandestine Literature in France 1769–1789, 1995, pp. 194, 199, 206, 227). P. 82: he accepts being judged ‘lacking in deference towards universally admired heroes of scholarship like Furet, Darnton, and Baker’ and seeks ‘to demonstrate the shortcomings of their ubiquitously venerated views’. Darnton is the one historian in the passage given a specific charge, so he alone is proposed. The polemic is Israel's; Darnton's books are unread here and no reply by Darnton was found. Distinct from edge_2867 (Israel ↔ Cambridge contextualism).

review.reason: H-France Forum 9:1 Israel response (publisher PDF; acceptable) re-read: p. 85 'Darnton, Chartier, Jacob, Goodman, Roche, Lilti, and others err in my estimation ... because they hardly engage with ideas at all'; 'Darnton’s treatment of d’Holbach whose books regularly topped his lists of the most widely selling clandestine texts, an astounding fact which, however, he completely ignores' (n. 25, Corpus of Clandestine Literature 1995); p. 82 'lacking in deference towards universally admired heroes of scholarship like Furet, Darnton, and Baker'. Page locators confirmed against the PDF running heads. Israel himself notes that Popkin, Gordon, Eisenstein and Curran make the same d'Holbach observation; optional to mention. Accept.

proposed_edges.relationship: De Dijn (2012) reads Israel's Enlightenment trilogy as reviving, ‘albeit in a dramatic new form’, the modernization thesis first formulated by Peter Gay, that the Enlightenment helped create modern liberal democracy
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A named reader, read 2026-10-31: Annelien de Dijn, ‘The Politics of Enlightenment: From Peter Gay to Jonathan Israel’, Historical Journal 55:3 (2012): 785–805, author abstract: the view that the Enlightenment played ‘a crucial role in the creation of the modern, liberal democracies of the West’ was ‘first formulated by Peter Gay’; ‘Jonathan Israel's trilogy on the Enlightenment has revived the modernization thesis, albeit in a dramatic new form’; yet even Israel's work ‘does not convincingly demonstrate’ the link. Israel himself cites this article (H-France Forum 9:1, 2014, n. 41, citing p. 799) when rejecting the claim of a consensus against him. Undirected comparison drawn by de Dijn: no personal debt from Gay to Israel is asserted, and the article body is unread. Pocock's disputing of Gay's unified Enlightenment (Israel 2016 abstract) is a separate matter for Gay's entry.

review.reason: de Dijn, Historical Journal 55:3 (2012), author abstract (Crossref) re-read: modernization thesis 'first formulated by Peter Gay'; 'Jonathan Israel's trilogy on the Enlightenment has revived the modernization thesis, albeit in a dramatic new form'; Israel's work 'does not convincingly demonstrate' the link. Israel's H-France response n. 41 cites de Dijn p. 799 (verified). Undirected comparison, attributed to de Dijn, no personal debt asserted; structure correct (directed false, type connection). Accept.

Held: an edge would rest on a list mention; the reviewer may decide to add Chartier if Israel's critique of Cultural Origins of the French Revolution can be read.

Israel distances his ‘controversialist method’ from context ‘in the manner of the “Cambridge school”’ (H-France 2014, p. 78); La Vopa (HJ 2009, n. 6) cites Skinner's ‘Meaning and understanding’ as the locus classicus. Already represented by edge_2867 (Israel ↔ context); no personal exchange with Skinner found.
